summary: Moses ascends with replacement tablets, and God proclaims mercy, faithfulness, forgiveness, and continuing judgment before renewing covenant commands. After forty days Moses returns with the tablets and a shining face, instructs the people, and uses a veil between his encounters and speeches.
whyItMatters: Renewal follows the calf crisis through a fresh declaration of God's character and renewed obligations of exclusive worship. Mercy does not erase the chapter's troubling language about punishment across generations or its demands concerning other peoples' worship.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: A renewed solitary ascent of Sinai and Moses' return to the waiting Israelite community.
context.literaryForm: Divine self-proclamation, intercession, a renewed covenant command collection, and a shining-face narrative.

before.text: Moses has secured a promise of divine presence and asked to see God's glory. The protected encounter now unfolds with new tablets and the proclamation of the name.

here.text: The chapter joins mercy and judgment, restates covenant obligations after the calf, and ends with the people receiving commands from a visibly changed mediator.

after.text: Moses assembles the community, reiterates Sabbath, and invites willing gifts and skilled work to build the sanctuary.

outline.heading: Replacement tablets and solitary ascent
outline.note: Moses prepares stones and follows the renewed mountain boundaries.

outline.heading: The name proclaimed and pardon requested
outline.note: Mercy and judgment are announced, and Moses asks God to remain among the people.

outline.heading: Covenant and exclusive worship
outline.note: The commands join promised marvels and displacement with rejection of other worship and cast idols.

outline.heading: Festivals, firstborn, rest, and offerings
outline.note: The calendar and gifts renew recurring covenant obligations.

outline.heading: Writing and forty days
outline.note: Moses receives writing instructions and remains without food or water during the encounter.

outline.heading: The shining face and veil
outline.note: Moses communicates the commands, and the veil marks his movement between encounters and the community.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
keyVerses.why: The divine proclamation begins with mercy, grace, patience, and abundant kindness and truth.

keyVerses.text: keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
keyVerses.why: Forgiveness and refusal to clear guilt stand together with a difficult statement about later generations.

keyVerses.text: Afterward all the children of Israel came near, and he gave them all the commandments that Yahweh had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.
keyVerses.why: The renewed encounter results in commands transmitted to the whole community.

questions.question: What links the new tablets to the broken ones?
questions.answer: God tells Moses to chisel two like the first and promises the same words that were on those Moses broke. The renewed encounter restores continuity with the covenant while openly naming its earlier rupture.

questions.question: Does the proclamation describe only forgiveness?
questions.answer: It names mercy, grace, patience, kindness, truth, and forgiveness, but also refuses to clear guilt and speaks of visiting ancestors' iniquity on later generations. Both sides belong to the proclamation, leaving a real tension about inherited consequences alongside its promise of forgiveness.

questions.question: What does “jealous” mean in the covenant warning?
questions.answer: It expresses God's demand for exclusive worship and rejection of rival divine allegiance. The surrounding commands concern covenants, sacrifices, family connections, and idols that might draw Israel into serving other gods.

questions.question: What happens to the worship sites of the land’s inhabitants?
questions.answer: Israel is ordered to break altars and pillars and cut down Asherah poles, while God promises to drive out named peoples. This is a program of religious destruction and displacement within the covenant speech, alongside its warning against adopting other worship.

questions.question: Must work stop even during urgent agricultural seasons?
questions.answer: Yes. The Sabbath command expressly includes plowing and harvest, the periods when field work might appear especially pressing. The festival calendar also ties the community's year to departure from Egypt and the gathering of produce.

questions.question: How are human and animal firstborn treated?
questions.answer: Firstborn cattle and sheep belong to God; a donkey is redeemed with a lamb or has its neck broken. Firstborn sons must be redeemed, an explicit distinction that prevents the command from being read as an order to sacrifice the children.

questions.question: Who is said to write the renewed covenant words?
questions.answer: Verse 1 promises God's writing on the tablets, while verse 27 commands Moses to write these words. Verse 28 then says he wrote the covenant words, the ten commandments; the passage places divine and mediated writing together without fully spelling out their relation at each step.

questions.question: When does Moses wear the veil?
questions.answer: He puts it on after speaking to the people, removes it when going before God, and then comes out to report the commands with his shining face visible. The veil is restored until the next encounter; the chapter does not say he keeps it on while delivering the commands.

glossary.def: Provide the required substitute or release, explicitly required here for firstborn sons.
Cult objects associated with the inhabitants’ worship that Israel is ordered to cut down.
The face covering Moses uses between speaking encounters after the people see his radiance.
